title: Boléro: Ravel (1930) and Fricsay
question: How does the chosen pulse change the progression from solo flute to the final brass and percussion?
intro: A snare drum starts its two-bar pattern, and a flute begins the tune of Boléro. In 1930 Ravel recorded the long crescendo with the Lamoureux Orchestra; Fricsay conducts the Berlin orchestra in the second performance. The flute enters quietly, and the crescendo runs until the trombones and percussion play the ending.

recordings.label: Maurice Ravel, Lamoureux Orchestra, 1930
recordings.note: The composer conducted the Lamoureux Orchestra for Polydor in January 1930.

recordings.label: Ferenc Fricsay, Berlin Symphonic Orchestra
recordings.note: Fricsay conducts Berlin’s orchestra in a recording restored by Pablo Varela in 2015.

passages.label: Opening flute melody
passages.note: A solo flute plays the first tune above the snare drum and plucked strings. The bass alternates C and G.

passages.label: First melody, oboe d’amore
passages.note: The oboe d’amore brings back the first melody. The bassoons take over the drum’s rhythm and the strings continue pizzicato.

passages.label: Horn, celesta and two piccolos
passages.note: A horn plays the tune beneath celesta and two piccolos. Their notes at different heights combine into one voice.

passages.label: Modulation to E major
passages.note: The bass finally leaves C, and the orchestra moves to E major. The drum’s two-bar rhythm continues through the sudden change.

passages.label: Return to C major and close
passages.note: C major returns with trombone slides. Bass drum, cymbals and tam-tam join the last six bars, and the orchestra brings the dance to a halt.
